claim: Technical Architecture §: time is encoded as audio by biphase mark code — 'every bit boundary gets a clock transition; a mid-cell transition also occurs for a 1'. Open Questions asks 'Can you hear LTC?' and guesses LTC cannot be read backward; LTC's asymmetric sync word exists so readers can tell direction, and readers do decode it in reverse and at shuttle speeds, so a decode-reversed piece would answer the page's own question (latent error).

pieces.what: An inline LTC encoder: type a timecode, see its 80 bits (BCD fields, user bits, the sync word) and the biphase mark waveform, hear it on a click; tests 'every bit boundary gets a clock transition; a mid-cell transition also occurs for a 1' and 'a self-clocking waveform carries both timing and data' by decoding its own audio back to the bits.

Encode a run of frames, play it, then decode it forward, reversed and at shuttle speeds with a transition-timing reader; the asymmetric sync word (0011 1111 1111 1101) is what tells direction. Answers 'can it be read backward' with a count of frames recovered each way, and 'can you hear it' by playing it.
pieces.walks_up_from: the 16-bit sync word, forward and mirrored

pieces.what: A drop-frame counter at 29.97 across a minute boundary showing the skipped frame numbers (00 and 01 dropped except every tenth minute), with the wall-clock error it corrects.
